The stages and their structure ​

The foundations state when a redistribution of weighted markers is symplectic, in the three forms of the condition (full space, leaf of constant weights, pseudo-time flow), and why a map that moves each marker on its own keeps every hole (uncoupled maps). Suites 1 and 2 of the structural suites check the three forms with ForwardDiff Jacobians and with controls that drop the recoil or read at fixed . This page adds what the stages of the sliced map do: coupling the markers is not enough to fill a hole, the sliced lift is a global symplectic diffeomorphism, the weight squeeze is a linear canonical map that keeps the total momentum, the composed map satisfies  , and a later flow step with weights read from the state has a composition defect.

Coupling is necessary, not sufficient ​

A canonical map of all markers keeps the volume of , not that of the single-marker space, so a map that couples the markers is free of the obstruction of uncoupled maps. Coupling is necessary but not sufficient: the one-slice lifts of the checkerboard couple all markers and still leave the empty quadrants empty. For a large number of markers in one slice, the quantile lift approaches a map of each marker's own coordinate (its rank becomes its quantile), and the obstruction applies in that limit; this is a heuristic reading, not a statement proved here. The slices break it: within a slice of small velocity range the positions are spread over the whole interval, whatever their correlation with the velocity.

Slices that depend on the state

The sliced map reads its slices, their order and the anchors from the input state: velocity slices from the sorted velocities, position slices from the sorted output of . These are piecewise constant functions of the state. On every open set where no two markers swap their order the map is the smooth map of the proposition, so it is symplectic there. It jumps where the order changes. Whether the map with state-dependent slices is injective across these sets is an open question. A canonical map whose parameters are read from the data is a weak statement for a finite marker set (finite marker sets); the content of the proposition is that each lift is one smooth map of all markers for its frozen data.

Quantile limit. For    and   with a slice ordered like its centred targets, the mollified sign tends to  ,   and the sum becomes   :   , the quantile map onto the targets, shifted to the mean. This one-dimensional quantile map is the optimal transport map of the slice for a convex cost (Villani, 2009). For   the lift relaxes towards it: the slice means by the factor towards the global mean, the deviations within a slice by towards the targets. The constant is the positive root of     with   ; it compensates in part the attenuation of the mollified sign and tends to 1 as  . Any positive constant keeps the proposition true. The test test/sliced/lift.jl checks the limit to for  .

Composition with a later flow step ​

A redistribution is followed by time steps of the marker dynamics, whose Hamiltonian depends on the weights,     , and which keep the weights (the second of the two readings). Symplectic integrators keep the canonical form of at fixed parameters (Marsden and West, 2001; Hairer et al., 2006); here the parameters come from the remap. The proposition below has the form of the closed-loop identity, with the weights in the role of the parameters and the exact flow in place of one step.
